articles.title_orig: Raoni Barcelos Hospitalized After Leaving UFC Fight Night Main Event on Stretcher
articles.title_zh: Raoni Barcelos Hospitalized After Leaving UFC Fight Night Main Event on Stretcher
articles.content_orig:
UFC fighter Raoni Barcelos was hospitalized at a Level 1 trauma center in the aftermath of Saturday's loss to Raul Rosas Jr.
UFC released a statement that said Barcelos was "stable, alert and responsive, with full movement" after undergoing a CT scan.
As ESPN's Jeff Wagenheim described, Barcelos "appeared to lose consciousness after a fifth-round takedown and was carried from the cage on a stretcher" at the end of the UFC Fight Night matchup in Las Vegas.
Wagenheim noted Barcelos' coach, Davi Ramos, provided an update on Saturday as well and said, "everything is fine, everyone can stay calm."
As for the fight itself, Rosas was trailing heading into the final round but was more aggressive toward the end. After he slammed Barcelos to the mat, the referee stopped the fight when it seemed as if the 39-year-old was unconscious.
Rosas, who became the youngest fighter to ever sign with UFC at 17 years old in 2022, has now won six fights in a row.
However, he was focused on his opponent in the aftermath as well.
"I want everybody tonight to please pray for Raoni Barcelos," he said in his postfight interview to the crowd. "Man, he's a warrior. It takes two to tango."
UFC's statement said Barcelos "will remain under medical supervision. We will provide updates on his condition as they become available."

articles.title_orig: Knicks star Jalen Brunson shows some solid comedy chops in as 'SNL' season opening host
articles.title_zh: Knicks star Jalen Brunson shows some solid comedy chops in as 'SNL' season opening host
articles.content_orig:
NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson, of the 2026 championship-winning New York Knicks, kicked off the 52nd season of “Saturday Night Live.”
During Saturday’s hoops-heavy show, Brunson delivered a monologue in which he promised to approach his “SNL” performance with the same strategy he used during the Knicks’ Finals games.
“The first three quarters of the show are going to be god-awful,” he said. “The last sketch is going to be amazing.”
The monologue featured “SNL” veteran Kenan Thompson as ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith, invited by Brunson so the player could “get some closure” after Smith had expressed doubts about his abilities.
Jalen Brunson brings Knicks players to 'SNL'
“I am man enough to admit that I was wrong when the New York Knickerbockers signed you and I did not think that you were the answer,” Thompson’s Smith said. “Nor did I believe that you could deliver the team’s first championship since 1973, when I was only 5 years old.”
Knicks teammates Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, Mikal Bridges and Karl-Anthony Towns made cameos to portray members of the studio audience chosen to ask questions of the point guard.
“Can you foul out of ‘SNL’?” Towns asked.
In the recorded sketch “High School Musical the New Generation,” Brunson played a new student who wanted to join the school’s basketball team. He was welcomed with a musical number on the court that culminated with a team member portrayed by “SNL” featured player Jeremy Culhane singing that he was about to “take the shot.”
It was at that point that his attempt at scoring was rejected by Brunson, with the ball slamming against his forehead. Each subsequent attempt at a basket by Culhane’s character was met with an over-the-top rejection. Soon, Brunson was defeating the team by weaving through defender traffic and scoring easily.
The NBA player concluded by swooping in to steal Culhane’s love interest (played by featured player Veronika Slowikowska) during another musical number, showing that even his singing chops were better than Culhane’s character’s. “Yeah, I think I’m going to hook up with this guy,” Slowikowska’s character said of the new student.
Brunson is the fifth NBA star to host the storied sketch comedy show, joining coach Bill Russell and legendary players Michael Jordan, Charles Barkley and LeBron James in sharing that status.
He averaged 32.6 points per game in the NBA Finals to help his team win its first championship in 53 years.
Saturday’s show also marked the first “SNL” season for two new featured players , Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter, after it bid farewell to cast member Chloe Fineman and writer Martin Herlihy, who also appeared in a number of sketches.
Fineman landed a role on “Myron Bolitar,” a Netflix drama series based on Harlan Coben’s thriller novels about a former basketball star who reinvents himself as a sports agent. Netflix announced the show started filming in New York City in July.
The musical guest Saturday was Katseye, the K-pop-influenced act composed of six women from around the world but often performing as a quintet and quartet due to hiatuses. The act was put together under a partnership between Geffen Records and South Korea’s HYBE Entertainment, home of BTS.
Katseye performed a pair of songs, “Animal” and “Hootie Frutti,” and appeared as judges in a recorded sketch that spoofed Season 2 of the talent competition TV show “The Debut: Dream Academy.”
“SNL” airs on NBC, a division of NBCUniversal, which is also the parent company of NBC News.

articles.title_zh: Raoni Barcelos’ coach shares medical update after scary UFC Vegas 121 fight ending
articles.content_orig:
Raoni Barcelos lost a UFC main event fight to Raul Rosas Jr. in Las Vegas
The UFC Vegas 121 main event clash between Raoni Barcelos and Raul Rosas Jr. ended in scary fashion in the fifth round when the Brazilian bantamweight went unconscious for apparent no reason during a clinch exchange. Barcelos was rushed to the hospital for exams after the bout, and his head coach Davi Ramos shared on social media he is now back to his senses.
The UFC released a statement hours after the incident to confirm Barcelos was transported to a Level 1 trauma center for evaluation and was “stable, alert and responsive, with full movement” after a “CT scan and comprehensive assessment” were conducted.
“Raoni is doing well,” Ramos said in Portuguese on a video posted on social media. “He has all his senses, he’s moving his leg, his arm, his hand, he’s conscious, he’s talking, everything is fine with him. He’s undergoing some tests, and pretty soon he’ll be here to talk to you guys.”
“I just wanted to let you know so you can all stay calm,” he continued. “Keep praying for him. He’s undergoing all the tests that are standard in a situation like this. He’ll have to rest because of what happened, but God willing, everything will be fine. He’ll be here with us soon and he’ll be talking to you guys. Thank you to everyone who’s been sending messages, positive energy, praying and keeping all of us in your prayers.”
Barcelos was up in all three scorecards going into the final round, including a 10-8 in round four for one of the judges, meaning he was a little over three minutes away from a decision victory. The loss snapped what would be his sixth straight victory in the UFC.
“We had a great fight,” Ramos said. “We practice a sport that we can’t predict, unfortunately, but we know for sure that we were doing our best. Raoni is a warrior, a phenomenal fighter, and he showed you that with all the technique he has, all the skill and heart he has. He showed everything about where he wants to go, where we all want to go, with all the work we’ve been putting in. Congratulations to him, and thank you all for the messages. Keep praying for him, and pretty soon he’ll be back here with us to put on another great show.”

articles.title_orig: From professor to patient: One man's journey on the frontier of lung cancer treatment
articles.title_zh: From professor to patient: One man's journey on the frontier of lung cancer treatment
articles.content_orig:
Dr. Bryant Lin teaches a lung cancer class in fall 2024. He says he was very nervous to teach the first class and share his story. The Lin family hide caption
Stanford medical professor Bryant Lin founded the school's Center for Asian Health Research and Education , advocating for better lung cancer screening in particular. Then two years ago Lin became a Stage IV patient of the very disease he long crusaded against.
"Super ironic that I would be co-leading the center that supports research and education in this disease, and I get diagnosed myself," he says.
Lin, who is a non-smoker, tells students he considers himself lucky — even hopeful: "I think the future is really bright, because we're creating all of these personalized, specialized precision therapeutics for lung cancer," he says."My hope is if we're not able to cure lung cancer, we can at least turn it into a chronic disease."
Notable improvements are shifting the prognosis for a disease once considered a death sentence. Much of the recent progress is so new, it is only starting to shift the statistics on survival. While the five-year survival rate across all stages of lung cancer has doubled in three decades, it still remains at a low 30%. (Stage of disease makes a huge difference; early, localized cancer survival rates over 5 years was 67% between 2015 and 2021.)
The genetics of lung cancers are very diverse and complex relative to other cancers, making it historically tricky to treat. One key technological development underlying many new treatments is the ability to identify, through genetic testing, the specific mutation driving a person's abnormal cell growth, according to UCLA oncologist and researcher Jonathan Goldman . "We can pick a drug that's really been developed for that type of cancer," he says.
Not only can that manage or even shrink tumors, because the drugs are better targeted, they also cause less collateral damage, making side effects typically more tolerable for patients.
"Survival used to be under a year, and now it's often several years and sometimes many years," Goldman says.
Whether it's breast, liver or lung cancer, targeting treatments by genetic subtype is far more effective than generalized treatments of the past, Goldman says, because the medicines are designed to focus their attack on specific mutated cells driving the abnormal growth. Since the medicines are targeted, they also tend to have fewer harsh side effects compared to chemotherapy.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter .
Tests to identify a patient's specific cancer subtype – a procedure called comprehensive genomic testing – are already available, and Goldman served as principal investigator on a recent study published in the New England Journal of Medicine , showing dramatic reductions in recurrence, when patients with rare subtypes receive targeted medicines as their first treatment.
However, access to such testing is spotty. Goldman says fewer than half of lung-cancer patients in the U.S. get their cancer genetically tested prior to treatment because that evaluation is not yet considered "standard of care." Plus, doctors themselves may not be aware it exists; Goldman says treatment technology is changing so rapidly, general oncologists may not be up-to-date on some of the most recent developments specific to lung cancer.
"The next step is not just these scientific discoveries, but learning how to implement these findings," he says. "We've proven time and time again how important and effective it is to get this testing done early so you can pick your best treatment first."
It was one of those relatively new targeted drugs, a daily pill called Tagrisso (or osimertinib), that professor-patient Bryant Lin initially began taking when he was first diagnosed in May 2024. Just three months prior to that, the Food and Drug Administration approved its use in combination with chemotherapy , based on data showing it lengthened survival.
"I am a beneficiary of years – of decades – of research," Lin says, noting how his treatment regimen has closely mapped with some of the most recent drug developments. "Since I've been diagnosed. It's quite amazing how quick – how rapid – our advances have been occurring."
Treatment is one thing; affording them is another. Even Lin, a patient with the unusual privilege of being a nationally known expert at an elite medical center, faces battles with insurance to get some of these new, expensive treatments covered. Insurers almost always require prior authorization for the treatments, or deny coverage for new drugs that haven't yet received expert endorsement as standard protocol. Lin says this happened for one of his $16,000 drugs, delaying his treatment at a critical time. He watches patients, too, fight similar battles over coverage.
"Oral drugs and the IV drugs — they're hundreds of thousands of dollars," he says. "I don't know too many people who could afford to pay out of pocket."
A year into his treatment, the initial targeted therapy Lin was taking stopped working. By then, regulators approved another drug combination – amivantamab and lazertinib – an antibody to activate the immune system, and a different pill targeting his specific mutation type, known as EGFR.
Dr. Bryant Lin receives a chemo infusion in the early days of his treatment in June 2024. The Lin family hide caption
Lin, who still teaches , travels, and advises the Susan Wojcicki Foundation for lung cancer, says these new therapies have given him both more life, and one of better quality. "My symptoms are really well controlled. I can live my life. I can speak. I don't think I've coughed once in our conversation."
What's more, there's a compounding effect with this kind of scientific progress, where recent breakthroughs with other genetically similar cancers may soon apply to lung cancer.
One promising area of potential crossover is with pancreatic cancer, which is driven by a gene in the same KRAS family that causes a sizable minority of lung cancers. One drug the FDA approved in August called Rasonque (generic name daraxonrasib), doubled survival for late-stage cancer patients to over 13 months in clinical trials – a rare victory against pancreatic cancer, a particularly stubborn form of the disease.
There are other promising drugs for pancreatic cancer that may eventually find application against lung cancer as well, including mRNA vaccines — custom designed to match the genetic profile of each individual's cancer. Researchers and companies say those show promise re-enlisting the immune system into fighting tumors.
"I've been investigating that for myself – personalized mRNA vaccine," Lin says.
Lin's professional focus remains on advocating for better modes and rates of screening, which remains at a stubbornly 18% among the high-risk patients for whom annual, low-dose CT scan screening (image tests) is the standard recommendation. But with screening, too, there is progress: AI imaging and increasingly sensitive blood tests may help detect, or even predict, formation of disease even years earlier.
Just as colorectal cancers can now be screened for using blood, stool and colonoscopy tests, Lin wants to see options besides the CT scan for lung cancer. Expanding these kinds of surveillance technologies could ultimately do more to reduce lung cancer deaths.
Lin himself is like a trapeze artist, grabbing hold from one treatment to the next. A fellow cancer patient told him: All he needs is to do is hang on. "He says, 'Hey, you only need to survive long enough until the next new treatment comes out' – and that's been the case for me," Lin says. His life of limbo involves balancing acts – as doctor and patient, as optimist and realist. "I'm hopeful," he says. "But, absolutely: The odds are against me."

articles.title_zh: We're Witnessing the Stock Market Do Something for Only the 3rd Time in 156 Years, and History Is Crystal Clear About What's Next for Stocks
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
For the better part of the last four years, Wall Street's bull market has been unstoppable. Aside from the short-lived tariff tantrum in April 2025 and a brief pullback associated with the Iran war earlier this year, the time-tested Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI), benchmark S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), and tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) have all blasted to several record highs this year.
Catalysts have been abundant and include (but aren't limited to):
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
The artificial intelligence infrastructure build-out
Considerably better-than-expected corporate earnings
Record share repurchases by S&P 500 companies
History-making initial public offering activity
While more than a century of history has decisively shown that Wall Street's major stock indexes rise over extended periods, things may not be as ideal as the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite make them appear.
Image source: Getty Images.
Currently, we're witnessing the stock market do something that's only been accomplished three times over the last 156 years . When this signal appears, it has consistently foreshadowed significant declines to come for Wall Street.
Make no mistake about it, there are always headwinds threatening to end Wall Street's bull market, such as rapidly rising margin debt and the potential for an extended Fed rate-hiking cycle. But if history repeats, it's premium stock valuations that offer the direst outlook for the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500, and Nasdaq Composite.
To be upfront, "valuation" is a tricky subject. Without a one-size-fits-all blueprint for evaluating and valuing individual companies or the broader market, it's not uncommon for emotions or subjectivity to factor into the equation. Subjectivity and emotion are what make it virtually impossible to accurately forecast short-term directional moves in individual stocks or major stock indexes.
There is, however, one valuation tool that, when backtested, has demonstrated an uncanny ability to accurately forecast the future for Wall Street's major indexes. I'm talking about the S&P 500's Shiller Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio, which is also known as the Cyclically Adjusted P/E Ratio (CAPE Ratio).
The Shiller P/E Ratio is based on average inflation-adjusted earnings over the previous 10 years. Accounting for a decade of earnings history ensures that recessions won't render this valuation tool useless, as can sometimes happen with the traditional P/E ratio when earnings (briefly) turn negative.
Economists introduced the CAPE Ratio in the late 1980s and have backtested it as far back as January 1871. Over this roughly 156-year stretch, the average multiple is 17.42. As of the closing bell on Sept. 21, the S&P 500's CAPE Ratio clocked in at 41.60.
Including the present, there have only been three times, spanning 156 years, in which the S&P 500's Shiller P/E Ratio has topped 40 -- and the previous two occurrences were followed by notable bear markets:
January 1999 to September 2000 : The Shiller P/E Ratio reached its record high of 44.19 in December 1999, mere months before the dot-com bubble officially burst. After spending the better part of two years with a Shiller P/E above 40, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite lost 49% and 78% of their values by October 2002, respectively.
January 2022 : For only a few days during the first week of 2022, the S&P 500's CAPE Ratio exceeded 40. Shortly thereafter, the 2022 bear market took shape, eventually wiping away a fifth, a quarter, and a third of the Dow's, S&P 500's, and Nasdaq's respective values over nine months.
May 2026 to present : Although the Shiller P/E Ratio briefly poked its head above 40 several times last year and earlier this year, it's been consistently above this mark since May 2026.
History doesn't mince its words: Premium stock valuations aren't well-tolerated over an extended period. When the S&P 500's CAPE Ratio tops 40, history foreshadows nothing short of a bear market.
Image source: Getty Images.
For short-term traders and those trying to time the market, history probably isn't your friend right now. But for investors who can take a step back and examine the bigger picture, history is often their greatest ally.
To be clear, stock market corrections and bear markets are an inevitable aspect of the investing cycle and should be viewed as the price of admission to one of the world's greatest wealth creators. But just because the Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq occasionally move lower, it doesn't mean bull and bear markets are linear.
According to Bespoke Investment Group, there's a mile-wide disparity between S&P 500 bull and bear markets. Whereas the average bear market over the last 97 years has found its trough in an average of 286 calendar days (about 9.5 months), the typical S&P 500 bull market has persisted 3.6 times as long (1,023 calendar days).
But the real merit of patience is seen in a data set refreshed annually by analysts at Crestmont Research. Crestmont examined the rolling 20-year total returns, including dividends, of the benchmark S&P 500 since 1900. Even though the S&P didn't officially exist until 1923, researchers were able to track its components in other major indexes as far back as the turn of the century.
Crestmont's analysis yielded 107 rolling 20-year periods through 2025 (1900-1919, 1901-1920, and so on, through 2006-2025). What's noteworthy is that all 107 generated a positive annualized return. In simpler terms, if an investor had purchased an S&P 500 tracking fund (note: S&P 500 index funds weren't available on U.S. exchanges until 1993) at any point from 1900 to 2006 and held for 20 years, they would have made money every time.
History and the power of perspective show that no matter what's thrown the stock market's way -- recessions, depressions, high inflation, wars, pandemics, Fed rate-hiking cycles, bubble-bursting events, and so on -- it has always motored higher over multiple decades. If the Shiller P/E accurately foreshadows a bear market once again, consider it a potential generational investment opportunity.

OpenAI has been at the centre of new concerns over uncontrolled AI activity
OpenAI has acknowledged that it alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been meddled with by its AI bots acting improperly.
AI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions", including the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Census Bureau and Education Department, the company said.
The disclosures come days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that OpenAI agents had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme.
Since August, public fears have grown over the potentially serious, even life-threatening, impacts of AI tools falling outside of human control.
OpenAI said that some of the data was accessed by AI agents, essentially bots that are designed and trained to operate somewhat autonomously, which were working to find "authoritative sources of public information".
But the company noted that some of the bots went beyond that and worked to bypass security measures on websites.
When attempting to get information from the Census Bureau, for instance, AI agents used tools reserved for software developers to access it, the company said.
OpenAI said all of the government data accessed by bots was public.
However, it noted that information that its bots accessed from the SEC, which regulates the US stock market and protects investors, was later published by AI agents on another website. OpenAI says this action was not intended.
In other instances that OpenAI disclosed on Friday, its AI agents transferred data when it should not have.
Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.
The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had opted in to allow OpenAI to train models using their data.
Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted: "This is not an appropriate use of this data."
It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.
Reuters first reported the expanded investigations. OpenAI also published details to its public blog.
In certain instances of the agent activity, OpenAI said the tools "bypassed" security controls of some websites.
In other instances, the AI agents showed "misalignment" in attempts to get at information from websites. Misalignment is a term used by AI companies and researchers to describe instances where an AI tool did something that it was not trained to do or was otherwise unintended.
OpenAI said that it was limiting identifying what entities were impacted because many had asked the company to not disclose details.
"Our goal is to give each organization the facts and defer to them on if and when to make the incident public," it said.
Not all of the instances involved in this incident were being considered a significant security breach, the company noted.
"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning," it explained. "Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address."
Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity, and how real are they?
Could AI wipe out humans and how might it do it?
The company said many of the incidents are being referred to as "agent spam", which it described as "unexpected or concerning" AI agent activity, like posting information to the internet.
OpenAI began taking such incidents more seriously after an incident in July where a group, or "swarm," of its AI agents hacked the AI developer platform Hugging Face without being prompted to do so.
Hugging Face was first to go public with the incident, with OpenAI publicly taking responsibility for it later.
Clement Delangue, the head of Hugging Face, during a United Nations Security Council session on AI on Wednesday: "I often wonder what would have happened had I decided not to disclose this attack publicly."
"Especially now that we know similar incidents had been happening months earlier in secret at a handful of frontier labs without monitoring," Delangue added.
During that same UN meeting, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, the head of rival firm Anthropic, asked for international leaders to form global standards for AI safety and ways to monitor and report such incidents.
Watch: What you need to know about the OpenAI Australian government hack
While OpenAI and Anthropic have both said in recent weeks that they will bring third-party evaluators inside their companies to do real-time safety evaluations of AI tools and models, such evaluators have not yet arrived, as the BBC has reported .
OpenAI said on Friday that it is currently reviewing training activity by its AI agents and going back on a "month by month" basis from when the Hugging Face hack occurred.
"Most cases identified so far have been low severity, with limited or no evidence of meaningful impact," the company said. "Given the scale of the review required, and the need to verify each case, this work will take months to complete."
David Krueger, a professor of machine learning at University of Montreal and the founder of AI safety group Evitable, said on Friday that he was "deeply troubled" by the increasing number of AI-related safety incidents.
He called for "an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium" on AI development.
"We have yet to understand the extent of existing incidents, and future rogue AI scenarios could be catastrophic," Krueger said.

articles.title_orig: Inside the workforce housing attracting Meta's data center workers
articles.title_zh: Inside the workforce housing attracting Meta's data center workers
articles.content_orig:
For decades, Richland Parish remained a small farming community nestled in Louisiana's northeast corner.
Residents living in the parish — a spattering of rural towns and unincorporated communities — had come to know their home for its slower pace of life. Much of the area is filled with winding back roads, sprawling farmland, and a skyline free of towering skyscrapers. The closest major regional city is Monroe, about 30 minutes west, with a population more than twice that of Richland Parish.
It's the kind of place where everybody claims to know everybody, or at very least, has heard of them. Now Meta has arrived , and things are changing.
In December 2024, the company announced plans to build its largest data center to date in Richland Parish, specifically near the unincorporated community of Holly Ridge, which local outlets report has fewer than 2,000 residents. Meta said the $50 billion, multi-year project would support around 7,500 jobs at the peak of construction and around 1,000 operational jobs, eclipsing the local community by thousands.
Angel Crawford of Delhi, a town about 10 minutes west of Holly Ridge, first noticed a surge in construction and operational workers arriving in her community last year.
Around that time, she and her husband, Bryan, opened a mobile home park to help address the housing gap.
Bryan and Angel Crawford initially worked in the nursing industry, but pivoted careers in 2024 after becoming empty nesters.
"We started with real estate and rentals because they are very much needed in this area," Angel told Business Insider. "It's very rural here, so when there are fluctuating prices in the market, it doesn't really hit us because there are never enough houses for sale or rent."
They began buying older homes and fixer-uppers that year.
"We had a vision to create a mobile home park, and already purchased some land when we heard about Meta's data center. That's what pushed us to keep going forward, " Angel said. "We understood there wasn't enough housing for residents, and our dream of building more multifamily houses was right in line to do that."
In 2024, the couple founded Parish Line Properties, which operates 18 homes in the area, including a mobile home park called Antley Pines. Of the 18 homes, 14 are considered workforce housing.
In many ways, Richland Parish is a microcosm of the debate about data centers across the US. Some Americans are optimistic about data centers, citing new jobs, revitalized economies, and the securing of the country's lead over China in AI development. Others are more critical, expressing concerns about the environment, the strain on utility grids, and how the acceleration of AI could impact the job market.
"Around here, people feel one way or the other about the data center. Either people are excited about the opportunities, or they hate them. There's no in between," Angel said. "I see it as an opportunity for us to have more experiences in our area and jobs for our children, so they can stay here instead of moving away."
The Crawfords opened Antley Pines in December 2025. Despite some locals' mixed feelings about the data center, the demand for housing is undeniable.
"All the homes were secured by deposits from Meta workers before we even got them into the park," Angel said.
She said many of her tenants are subcontractors, like electricians, working with Meta.
Although Antley Pines isn't directly in Holly Ridge, the mobile park is still reaping the economic benefits.
"Location is very important to Meta's workers because they work six to seven days a week and 12-plus hours a day. They leave around 4:30 in the morning, and they don't come home until 7 at night," Angel said.
That kind of routine can take a toll on workers, many of whom are not from the area.
"One of the big things my tenants tell me is that if they live in Dallas and it's 30 miles to work, it takes about 30 minutes. Well, in rural areas, 30 miles could take 60 minutes because of all the back roads and little towns you have to go through," she said. "The closer they can get to the job site, the better."
Antley Pines offers fully furnished four-bedroom, two-bathroom homes, which Angel said gives workers the option of staying with family or rooming with colleagues. She said the homes, which come with amenities, cost an average of $3,000 a month with utilities.
"I don't have any problem with getting tenants in those homes at that price point," Angel said. "Before Meta arrived, an unfurnished house without utilities in the same area would probably go for around $1,200 to $1,500 a month."
In Richland Parish, the median household income was around $53,000 in 2024.
"We've assured our local long-term tenants that we won't increase their rent. That's not what we're about. We're not going to put local tenants in a bind. We're going to find different and new properties to help with workforce housing," she said.
Angel said there are a few common requests among the construction and operational workers under Meta.
"As soon as they get into their rentals, 'What's the WiFi password?' is their first question," Angel said. "Some don't have their family here, so they want to do FaceTime."
The tenants also value an escape from the bustling construction site.
"They're with a lot of people all day long. They don't want to come home to a lot of noise," Angel said. "All of them say they love the peace and quiet."
The demand for lodging in the area has continued to grow, Angel said.
"I get phone calls or text messages almost daily. Most of them are from my current tenants who have met someone who's looking for somewhere to stay," she said. "If you go on any of the websites, like Realtor.com, not all local rental properties are listed on there."
That's what led her to create StayNELA, a third-party website connecting tenants with property owners in 2025.
"I did a lot of research for several months by driving around the area and looking at all the different signs in people's yards or at four-way stops that you couldn't read properly. I kept a log, took pictures, and kept them in a folder on my phone. If anything was on Facebook about a rental, I saved it."
While some construction workers traveled to work on Meta's data center, others were locals leveraging the opportunity that arrived in their backyard, Angel said.
"A lot of young men in this area work offshore at oil rigs, so it's a lot of time spent away from home," she said. "We know a lot of young people who are working at the construction site right now who would usually be off working away from home."
She added, "Hopefully, it'll bring more jobs to the area for our kids and grandkids."
Construction on Meta's data center is expected to continue for several years, but there's uncertainty among workers about how long they'll be in Richland Parish.
"Most of them don't know how long they're going to be here. They hope they're going to be here long-term, but in construction, they don't get told until it's done," Angel said.
Month-to-month leasing is among the top requests from tenants.
Although Meta's presence in Richland Parish has become the new normal, it won't last forever.
The data center will eventually become operational, meaning construction will wane, and workers will leave. The Crawfords have thought about a future without Meta, and they're not worried.
"Each home in our mobile park is on one-fourth of an acre. After Meta's gone, we can sell them individually or rent them out," Angel said.
For now, though, they're focused on the economic benefits that have come to Richland Parish from the data center project.
"We've seen a lot of laundromats, RV parks, and mobile home parks come to the area," Angel said. "It's great for the economy in our area because people who we've worked with who install electrical systems, septic systems, plumbing, gravel, and all those things are busy because Meta's here."

articles.title_orig: Where Republicans are playing offense ahead of the midterms
articles.title_zh: Where Republicans are playing offense ahead of the midterms
articles.content_orig:
The outcome of the 2026 election will be determined primarily by how well Republicans play defense across the growing list of GOP-held House and Senate seats Democrats are targeting. But the GOP is also hoping to play offense by flipping some House and Senate seats Democrats now control.
Because of their redistricting maneuvers, Republicans have more opportunities to flip House seats held by the other side than is typical for the president’s party in midterm elections. In the Senate, Republicans are seriously targeting four Democratic-held seats. But in both chambers, the same collapse in President Donald Trump’s approval rating that is threatening so many GOP incumbents is dimming the party’s prospects of unseating many Democrats.
The Republican financial advantage is large enough that the party can afford to force Democrats to commit resources defending seats they now hold — which is itself a benefit for the GOP. But it has never been easy during a midterm for the president’s party to flip seats held by the other side. And that has been especially true in midterms defined by a wave of discontent with the president’s performance — the conditions that appear to be coalescing this year.
Over nearly the past five decades, the party holding the White House has faced five full-scale wipeouts in House elections. Each time, while losing dozens of their own House seats, the president’s party has struggled to oust many legislators on the other side.
The president’s party flipped no more than four House seats held by the other side during the “wave” midterm elections under Ronald Reagan in 1982, Bill Clinton in 1994, Barack Obama in 2010 and Trump in 2018. In 2006, while losing the House under George W. Bush, Republicans did not capture a single Democratic-held seat. (Amid the more modest Democratic House losses in 2022 under Joe Biden, the party flipped four Republican-held seats.)
Republicans have legitimate reason to expect they can improve on that humble record this year. The National Republican Congressional Committee is officially targeting three dozen Democratic-held seats.
In this environment, Democrats don’t worry too much about Republicans defeating any of the dozen Democrats they are targeting in districts that voted for Kamala Harris in 2024. The major House race forecasters also generally give the GOP modest odds in those seats.
The core of this year’s GOP pick-up opportunity is the 22 Democrats running in seats that voted for Trump in 2024 . About two-thirds of those seats are in states where Republicans have redrawn the congressional maps to improve their chances.
After that gerrymandering offensive, the number of Democrats in Trump-won seats this year will roughly equal the 23 House Republicans who ran in 2018 in seats that voted for Hillary Clinton two years earlier.
Tracking states’ unprecedented redistricting efforts
In 2018, Democrats beat 20 of those 23 Clinton-district Republicans. That precedent undergirds the Republican optimism about flipping more seats than usual. “In 2018, Democrats took back their own turf,” says Mike Marinella, press secretary for the NRCC. “Now, in 2026, it’s almost the exact same situation on the other side as Democrats are the ones renting districts in Trump country, and we’re going all in to bring Republican voters home in November.”
But Republicans face many hurdles trying to match the overpowering Democratic 2018 performance in split-ticket districts. The GOP is strongly favored this year in the six seats where the new lines are forcing Democrats to run in districts that gave Trump about 57% of the vote or more (though Democrats and some independent analysts don’t entirely rule out an upset from Democratic incumbents Shomari Figures in Alabama and Darren Soto in Florida, or in an open seat around Houston).
The remaining 16 Democrats running in seats Trump won with 55% of the vote or less, though, are proving more competitive than many analysts initially expected. In 2018, Democrats looking to oust Republicans in districts that voted for Clinton had a huge tailwind of dissatisfaction with Trump. Conversely, Republicans looking to oust Democrats in districts that voted for Trump now face the headwind of discontent with the president.
CJ Warnke, communications director for House Majority PAC, the principal Democratic super PAC investing in House races, says that in the group’s polling, Trump’s approval rating “is underwater across the board, to varying degrees, in every district across the battlefield.” And that means even in districts Trump carried in 2024, association with him may be more anchor than sail in 2026.
The three heavily Latino South Texas Congressional districts that Republicans redrew in their gerrymander captures the GOP’s challenge. State Republicans reconfigured the Rio Grande Valley seats held by Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez and another Democratic seat south of San Antonio so that all three became districts where Trump carried about 55% of the vote in 2024 amid his sweeping gains among Latino voters.
But Trump’s support has eroded across the region. Recent polling by Texas Southern University found that about 55% of voters now disapprove of his performance in both the Cuellar and Gonzalez districts. (The poll didn’t include the San Antonio-area district.)
“It’s pretty obvious to anybody that does a poll that… the president’s popularity in South Texas is surely not what it was two years ago,” says Republican consultant Wayne Hamilton, who runs Project Red TX, an organization dedicated to growing the party in South Texas.

articles.title_orig: The other crop that built China: how millet became foundation for Chinese civilisation
articles.title_zh: The other crop that built China: how millet became foundation for Chinese civilisation
articles.content_orig:
While domestication of rice was crucial in southern China, it was millet that ruled the North, laying groundwork for birth of the country
Rice may be the most universal ingredient in the world, serving as a cornerstone of the diet for billions in Asia.
However, for much of Chinese history, rice faced a serious competitor, and entire cultures developed around a different cereal grain, one that has since diminished in significance: millet.
Millet is a cereal grain that behaves and tastes similarly to rice but has a rounder form. It is often used in porridge, stir-fries, or even fritters. In certain regions of China, millet is favoured as a food for pregnant women, with millet porridge being particularly gentle on the stomach. Despite this, it cannot rival the cultural importance of rice.
Yet, the domestication of millet, along with other cereals globally, stands as one of the most pivotal events in human history. Its domestication fundamentally altered natural landscapes and enabled humans to control the plants they consume, as opposed to surviving at the mercy of wild crops.

articles.title_orig: These Democrats are making Christianity a centerpiece of their midterm campaigns
articles.title_zh: These Democrats are making Christianity a centerpiece of their midterm campaigns
articles.content_orig:
Some Democratic candidates have made faith central to their congressional campaigns, including (from left) Frederick Haynes, Sarah Trone Garriott, James Talarico and Lindsay James. Getty Images, AP/Getty Images, AP hide caption
On a recent Sunday at Brentwood Baptist Church in Houston, James Talarico stood at the pulpit.
A state representative in the Texas House, Talarico is a former middle school teacher, a student at Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary and the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate.
"I want to speak to you this morning, not as a candidate, but as a fellow Christian," he told the congregation. "My grandad was a Baptist preacher in south Texas. And when I was real little, he told me that Christianity is a simple religion."
But it's not easy, Talarico continued, telling the congregation that faith could provide a way of understanding the country's political turmoil.
"Sometimes we see the world most clearly through our tears. If your heart is breaking as you watch what's happening to our beloved country, it means you still have a heart," he said. "So blessed are you who weep."
It's rare for Democrats to make religion a centerpiece of their campaigns. But this midterm election cycle, a number of candidates for Congress are doing just that. At least a half-dozen candidates are ordained clergy themselves; others are studying to become ministers. They include a megachurch pastor in Dallas, a Methodist minister in Kansas and two members of the clergy in Iowa – all of whom are in competitive races.
On the campaign trail, they've been invoking biblical teachings as they make the case for policies involving health care, veterans, immigrants and economic opportunity — while trying to persuade voters in states and districts where religion remains an important part of public life.
Republicans, meanwhile, have sharply criticized Democrats' religious rhetoric. Some have called the clergy running for office PINOs: Pastors In Name Only.
"I've never seen so much blasphemy from anyone running for office," Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick said of Talarico at the state Republican convention earlier this year. "And let me tell you what, I'm going to pray for that guy, because when he loses the Senate race, if he campaigns against God, as he's been doing, he's going to hell for sure."
Talarico has incorporated the attacks into his own campaign message.
"The real blasphemy is kicking the sick off their healthcare to fund tax cuts for billionaires," he told congregants at Brentwood Baptist.
Candice Stroud, who has been a member of the church for more than 40 years, said she appreciates Talarico's willingness to talk openly about Christianity.
"I think Democrats have been talking about religion for years. It's just nobody wants to listen to us if you don't say what they want to hear."
Asked whom she meant by "they," Stroud said: "The Republicans, basically. They don't want to hear that we are Christians. We go to church. We believe in the Bible."
'The most dangerous form of government'
Talarico is campaigning in a party whose voters are much less religious, on average, than Republicans. Pew Research Center's 2023-24 Religious Landscape Study found that 28% of Democrats and Democratic-leaning adults said religion was very important in their lives.
At a Democratic town hall later that afternoon, Talarico emphasized that his faith does not mean he wants religion to control government.
"My faith is central in my life," he said. "But I also know that the most dangerous form of government is theocracy. Because the only thing worse than a tyrant is a tyrant who thinks they're on a mission from God."
Talarico is a vocal opponent of Christian nationalism, a term commonly used to describe the belief that the United States is or should be a Christian nation and should promote Christianity. He has criticized the Trump administration over what he describes as the influence of the ideology.
"That is what we've seen from the Department of Defense," Talarico said. "We have seen Christian Nationalism infiltrate our Defense Department from Secretary Hegseth."
His Republican opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, has questioned Talarico's religious identity.
"We cannot let Texas turn based on a deceiver like James Talarico, who does not want the world to know who he really is," said Paxton speaking at a campaign rally this summer.
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Texas state Rep. James Talarico speaks at a food drive at the Frederick Douglass Human Services and Justice Center. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP hide caption
At the Democratic town hall in Houston, nearly 700 people filled the room. Many wore T-shirts or carried signs that read "Talarico for Texas" on the front and "Love Thy Neighbor" on the back.
Among those taking in the scene was Brandon Sterling, a 40-year-old nurse practitioner.
"I would say I'm more spiritual than religious, and the only thing I do religiously is I get up. I go to work. Go to the gym," he said lightheartedly.
But Sterling said he understands why Talarico is talking about faith.
"We're here in the South. You know, a lot of people lead their political views with their religious views. So if this is the voice or if this is how you have to reach the greatest amount of people, then so be it," Sterling said. "It doesn't offend me at all."
Madison Vega, a Democratic volunteer canvassing in Houston's Montrose neighborhood, said her grandfather, like Talarico's, was a Baptist preacher. She drifted away from religion after attending college, but said Talarico's approach to Christianity resonates with her.
"Part of the reason that I've kind of lost my closeness to the church is just that I kind of heard a lot of divisive messaging from church when I was growing up," Vega said. "And I like the way he doesn't use Christianity as a weapon."
But not everyone is receptive to the combination of religion and politics.
Kristin Kott, one of the voters Vega encountered while canvassing, said her main concerns are improving schools and recovering from recent flooding in her neighborhood.
"Talking about religion as it relates to policy and things like that, I would be turned off by," she said. "I don't think religion should play into government and politics at all. I thought the country was founded on that."
Talarico is not the only Democratic candidate using faith as part of a congressional campaign.
In Dallas, Frederick Haynes is the Democratic nominee for the U.S. House in District 30. He's led the 13,000-member Friendship-West Baptist Church for more than four decades.
Haynes says he was inspired to run after the Texas Legislature redistricted the state, eliminating one of its two predominantly Black U.S. House districts.
"I'm a Luke 4 Christian because Jesus says the spirit of the Lord is upon me because he's anointed me to preach good news to the poor," said Haynes, referring to a story in the Gospel of Luke where Jesus describes his authority to preach and teach.
"He prioritizes those who've been made poor by systems," he said. "Set the captives free. Heal those who are broken."
Similarly, Haynes sees his run for office as a way of doing the same: bringing concern for the poor and marginalized into the legislative process.
The Rev. Frederick Haynes III speaks to the crowd during the We the People TX interfaith service, "A Night of Moral Resistance," in Dallas in September. Gabriela Passos/AP hide caption
Haynes' Republican opponent, Everett Jackson, a local businessman and community leader, has attacked the pastor's religious sincerity.
"I cannot categorize him as a shepherd or a pastor," Jackson said on the conservative YouTube show Disturbing the Peace . "Because a shepherd – the good shepherd, as we're told by the Lord – they would see to the safeguarding of the sheep and lead them in the righteous path. This is not what Freddie Haynes is doing. Freddie Haynes has politicized the gospel and therefore misled his parishioners."

articles.title_orig: Russia intensifies hybrid war beyond Ukraine, rattling Europe
articles.title_zh: Russia intensifies hybrid war beyond Ukraine, rattling Europe
articles.content_orig:
The Kremlin is testing Europe ‘s limits.
After months of covert attacks and sabotage across the continent, leaders are warning that Moscow may be about to grow bolder as it seeks to sow chaos and intimidate allies of Ukraine .
Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve to defend members on its eastern flank or respond to attacks that fall short of all-out war, these officials say, at a time when the U.S. is distracted by other conflicts and weighing reducing its military presence in Europe.
An assessment by the Danish Defence Intelligence Service released Thursday warned that in the coming months Moscow will further intensify its campaign of so-called hybrid warfare , “with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past.” It also assessed “a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia.”
While Moscow has for years embraced tactics that straddle the threshold of war, a string of increasingly brazen incidents in recent months has alarmed U.S. allies.
A key moment was the discovery of a Russian drone carrying explosives at an airport in eastern Germany near a Ukrainian aircraft last month. Berlin formally blamed Russia for what it said was a thwarted attack and imposed a diplomatic freeze, though Moscow denied involvement.
That incident appears to have changed the mindset about Russia’s growing threat in Europe, said Ed Arnold, a senior associate fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank. “It just showed that Putin’s risk calculations are getting more liberal,” Arnold said. “Everyone just got a bit freaked out by that, quite frankly.”
It was followed by the unexpected visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow, during which NATO was discussed.
Incidents have continued to pile up — at defense facilities in Estonia, rail networks in Poland and the power grid in Germany. Many have passed without clear attribution, only intensifying speculation.
All this against the backdrop of near-daily drone incursions into European airspace, fueling anxiety in eastern border towns.
In Ukraine, a passenger train was hit less than 2 miles from the Polish border earlier this month, a close call on NATO’s doorstep that came as European diplomats returned from Kyiv on the same rail line. Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at the station when the drone struck.
Just days later, NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered the airspace of Lithuania, one of the Baltic member states whose proximity to Russia, analysts say, could make it a prime target for the Kremlin’s next move.
What could this look like? As unease increasingly swirled last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the Kremlin plans to launch drone and missile attacks against European countries that it would argue were accidental to try to weaken any response.
Russia has not claimed involvement in any of the incidents and has repeatedly denied conducting hybrid warfare or sabotage operations in NATO territory. Putin himself accused European leaders earlier this month of seeking out “a war against Russia” and “frightening their populations with an imaginary threat.”
On Friday, Russian state news agency RIA published and quickly deleted an op-ed laying out a potential scenario for a “lightning fast” war that Russia might wage against a NATO state, specifically focusing on the Baltic nations. The article was deleted because it did not “align” with editorial policy or Russia’s state policy, RIA said.
U.S. allies have little doubt that the broad pattern reflects the Kremlin increasingly pushing the boundaries.
“With these incidents now so frequent and so brazen, it is increasingly difficult to distinguish them from actual acts of war,” said Katja Bego, a senior research fellow with the Europe program at London-based think tank Chatham House. “The Kremlin is playing with fire here: The risk of more serious escalation — even if unintended — is very real.”
There is a mounting sense that something must be done, but what?
Lithuania has made plans for the evacuation of older adults and is lifting its ban on hosting nuclear weapons. Finland has warned citizens to be “mentally prepared” for new sabotage attacks. France is putting a plan in place to protect the country’s critical infrastructure.
Hanging over all of this is Article 5, NATO’s collective defense clause.
For Moscow, escalating hybrid attacks could highlight Western divisions over how best to respond and undermine the alliance at a time when the U.S. commitment to this mutual defense has been in question.
“I think they are trying to show Europe they can act without consequences, and more recently, to show Europe that the U.S. will not come to their rescue. It’s worrisome,” said William Alberque, a former senior NATO official based in Berlin.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Wednesday and told a media briefing that the U.S. was concerned that the Ukraine war could “metastasize and spread into other places ... be it through a hybrid attack, be it through a sabotage attack, be it through a misunderstanding.”
He added: “We watch reports carefully, and we raise them with the right people at the right levels.”
A State Department spokesperson told NBC News: “We continue to monitor Russia’s hybrid activities in Europe and are working closely with our allies and partners to strengthen resilience against the hybrid threat.”
Despite the spreading sense of alarm, some in Europe are urging against getting carried away.
NATO’s Baltic member states have not changed their security assessments, saying there is no imminent risk of a Russian invasion while much of Moscow’s military resources are tied up in Ukraine — and struggling to make progress there .
Latvia and Estonia directly border Russia, while Lithuania borders the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad. All three have been staunch supporters of Ukraine’s fight, driven in part by fears they could be next.
“Incursion of the type of 2022 Ukraine is not likely, let’s put it in a mild way,” Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs told reporters on the sidelines of this week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York. “Ukraine is fighting. Russia is absorbed in Ukraine. We do not observe any build-up near our borders,” Rinkēvičs added.
Neighboring Lithuania said this week a new rotation of U.S. troops was on its way to the country, ending uncertainty over a renewed deployment as the Pentagon weighs a broader plan to draw down U.S. forces on the continent.
“Russia’s pressure on Lithuania and other countries is not new,” Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas told NBC News, pointing to the decadelong Soviet occupation and adding that his country has more recently faced cyberattacks, disinformation and other forms of hostile influence from Moscow.
“There is no conventional threat at the moment,” Kaunas said via email, when asked why his country has not changed its security assessment. “At the same time, provocations and false-flag operations remain possible, and our intelligence points to increasingly aggressive Russian behavior. These are different threats, and they need different answers.”
But failing to take sufficient action could carry its own risks.
“Respond. Always respond,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged his European allies earlier this week.
“If you don’t respond to Russians, they will go further.”
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: Remote section of China’s Great Wall damaged by 20 years of mine waste dumping
articles.title_zh: Remote section of China’s Great Wall damaged by 20 years of mine waste dumping
articles.content_orig:
Whistle-blowers were repeatedly ignored as mining interests removed Ming dynasty stones to create a short cut to slag dump, CCTV reports
While foreign leaders and their families walk the iconic restored sections of the Great Wall around Beijing, the ancient stones of a remote Ming-era stretch of the structure in northern central China have been sacrificed for cheaper dumping of coal-mining waste.
For nearly 20 years, a section of the wall in Ningwu county, Shanxi province, was used as a short cut to dump slag, despite whistle-blowers repeatedly raising the alarm to officials, according to a report by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
The damage to the Great Wall’s Guojiayao section began in 2007, when an unlicensed miner, Ningwu Chaokai Coal Industry, dug a trench through the structure as a way to dispose of excavation waste, the report said.
In 2013, Shenda Chaokai Coal Industry was established through the consolidation of multiple mining teams and continued using the breach to dump slag, bypassing the long mountain roads.

articles.title_orig: Tensions run high in Northern Ireland after contentious march given go-ahead
articles.title_zh: Tensions run high in Northern Ireland after contentious march given go-ahead
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of protesters have blocked a route into the Catholic area of a Northern Irish town that a Protestant organisation was due to march down.
Northern Ireland’s High Court permitted the Protestant Orange Order organisation to march through a mainly Catholic area in the town of Portadown on Sunday for the first time in 28 years, reviving one of the region’s most contentious marching disputes.
The court rejected a final attempt by residents to stop the parade from passing through the Garvaghy Road, after Northern Ireland’s Court of Appeal overturned a temporary injunction granted on Saturday.
Thousands of people, including Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O’Neill of the Irish nationalist Sinn Fein and the party’s ‌leader, Mary Lou McDonald, gathered on the road to protest against the decision.
“This is madness,” McDonald told reporters shortly after 8am (07:00 GMT) when the march was due to begin. “This, in fact, is primitive treatment of any community in the year 2026. It is intolerable, and it will not be tolerated.
“This is a ⁠dignified and united community, and they are absolutely determined that ⁠they and we will not be drawn back into the past.”
McDonald and O’Neill urged the British government and police to intervene to stop the parade. O’Neill said she ⁠had spoken to Britain’s minister for the region and the Irish government.
Police vans parked nearby had earlier played out ⁠a warning that anyone taking part in the protest ⁠was committing a criminal offence.
A small group of Orange Order members wearing traditional silk orange sashes and black bowler hats gathered in another part of the town, a picture posted on X by Democratic Unionist Party ‌(DUP) lawmaker Carla Lockhart showed.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham called for calm, saying there have been “big gains made in Northern Ireland, and we don’t want to see things go backwards”.
Jon Boutcher, the head of Northern Ireland police, called for “those with influence to encourage people to comply with the law”, referring to the protest blocking the Garvaghy Road. He said there have been no signs of violence or disorder.
“Police are engaging and working with all parties and will continue to do so. It is incumbent on us all to come together at times like this to do all we can to preserve a peaceful Northern Ireland.”
Deputy First Minister Emma Little-Pengelly, from the DUP, which supports Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom, said on Sunday that threats of violence were unacceptable. “No one in Northern Ireland wants violence or disorder,” she added.
The Irish government said it was “very concerned” about the situation and that its priority was to avoid “a return to the divisions of the past”.
The Orange Order is a Protestant organisation closely associated with unionism, the political tradition that favours Northern Ireland remaining in the UK.
The Parades Commission, the independent body that rules on disputed marches in Northern Ireland, approved Sunday’s procession with a 35-person limit, barred bands and accompanying supporters, and required the march to finish by 9:30am (08:30 GMT).
The dispute over the Drumcree parade and Garvaghy Road became one of the most bitter marching confrontations of the “Troubles”, the decades-long conflict over Northern Ireland’s political status that largely ended with the 1998 Good Friday Agreement.
Repeated attempts by the Orange Order to return from Drumcree Parish Church along Garvaghy Road triggered protests, violence and major security operations during the 1990s.

articles.title_orig: A ‘Big Problem’: Trump’s War With Iran Drags Down Republicans in Midterms
articles.title_zh: A ‘Big Problem’: Trump’s War With Iran Drags Down Republicans in Midterms
articles.content_orig:
At least 17 members of Congress have called on the president to end the war.
Several Republicans running in competitive statewide and federal races are joining growing calls in their party to end the war in Iran with less than 40 days until the midterm elections.
As of Friday, 17 incumbent congressional Republicans running for re-election or non-incumbent candidates for Senate or governor's seats have called for an end to the war, either through votes in Congress to rein in President Donald Trump’s war powers or in statements on the campaign trail or online.
This comes as diesel fuel prices have jumped by nearly 60% since the conflict began at the end of February and as voters sour on the president -- a CNN poll conducted last week found 67% of Americans disapproved of Trump's job performance and 73% disapproved of how he was handling the situation in Iran. And 73% of Americans said that the war with Iran was having a negative effect on their financial situation, including 59% of Republicans.
Since the war in Iran started, Congress has voted on resolutions calling on Trump to get Congress' approval to continue hostilities in Iran. Of the 20 resolutions voted on, some Republicans have voted with Democrats five times to pass resolutions, though they don't force the president to do anything.
The GOP candidates who have broken with Trump on the war include six incumbent members of Congress running for reelection and five Republicans running in statewide races. Four of those five are currently in Congress and have voted against the war powers resolutions.
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, a former congressman, cut an ad on Monday saying, "The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly. When it does, energy costs will plummet." He has since said that any deal to end the war must ensure Iran can't build a nuclear weapon, Trump's stated goal for the conflict.
In Wisconsin, Rep. Tom Tiffany, the GOP nominee for governor, told ABC affiliate WISN on Wednesday, "it's time to move on."
"The president has final say in regards to this, but I just believe that we should be exiting Iran -- that it's time to move on," Tiffany said. "We've degraded their nuclear facilities. We degraded their military. Most of their ships are in the bottom of the ocean. Time to come home, take care of business here in America."
Tiffany's opponent, Democrat Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, put out an ad this week that slammed the congressman for voting in lockstep with the president on the war.
"Five times he has had the chance to end the war that’s driving our prices up, and five times he’s chosen Trump instead. Tom Tiffany’s only loyal to Trump -- not us, Wisconsin,” Crowley said in a press release.
Ohio Republican Sen. John Husted, facing a tight race for reelection, told Politico on Tuesday, "The war needs to come to an end as quickly as possible so that we can lower gas prices," but he again voted against a war powers resolution on Thursday.
Iowa Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, who's running in a tight Senate race, has voted against war powers resolutions, but reversed her position on Monday, calling for an "immediate end" to the war.
"Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran," she wrote. "We need to use every option at our disposal to provide some relief from high prices. … These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP, and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”
A day later, she insisted the House return to Washington, D.C. to address rising fuel prices, promising to "work with anyone to deliver."
“The House should return to DC immediately to work to pause diesel exports, suspend the gas tax, fully unleash E15 and biodiesel, and work on a diesel relief program for truckers and farmers," Hinson wrote on X .
House Speaker Mike Johnson last week canceled the two remaining weeks of its session and let the House leave early, saying, "It's time for our members to go home to their districts and make their case to the American people to go and explain all the great things we've done."
Hinson's Democratic opponent Josh Turek, a state lawmaker, responded on X , "It's easy to send a tweet but when you had the chance to vote to end this war, you chose not to. You voted seven times to continue it, including just last week."
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries criticized the Republicans who have recently broken with Trump on the war during a news conference Wednesday, saying that several of them are "on the verge of losing."
"Where were these Republican sycophants over the last six-plus months?" he said.
Iowa Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, who had opposed the war powers resolution but voted in favor of it last week, said in a statement, "Americans do not want another forever war."
She cited her military service and acknowledged the rising gas prices driven by the war in Iran, saying that Iowans are "paying too much at the pump."
And Iowa Republican Rep. Zach Nunn voted against previous war powers resolutions but broke with the president on the most recent vote.
"Iowa has already paid a devastating price, including two service members killed by an Iranian drone in Kuwait."
Nunn also recently demanded action on diesel prices, writing on X on Monday , "My plan: Sell American energy to Americans first. Pass my Iowa-led biofuel bill = bring down gas 50 cents. Hold Big Oil accountable for gouging," Nunn wrote.
ABC News' Lalee Ibssa, Jonathan Parker, Laura Peller and John Parkinson contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Bill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulation
articles.title_zh: Bill Gates says unchecked AI could ‘cause a billion deaths’ in call for regulation
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist speaks with NBC’s Kristen Welker in interview airing on Sunday
Bill Gates has called on the US’s federal legislators and law enforcers to regulate the development of artificial intelligence ( AI ), saying in an interview airing on Sunday that the technology left unchecked could cause “a billion deaths” and “no one thinks self-regulation is enough”.
“You need law enforcement and the politicians to get into the discussion about what safeguards and monitoring look like,” the Microsoft co-founder and philanthropist said to Kristen Welker, the NBC Meet the Press host. “And that has to be a required thing.”
Using a term meant to describe an expense required to run a business, Gates continued: “It will be a little bit of overhead for the industry – but not a dramatic slowing of what they’re doing.”
Another portion of the interview – excerpts of which NBC circulated in advance – saw Gates dramatically warn that AI in the wrong hands would be “certainly powerful enough to drive events that, you know, cause a billion deaths”.
“There’s never been a weapon as powerful as the combination of people with ill intent using the latest AI tools,” Gates added, echoing other recent similar warnings by a wide array of tech and political figures.
Gates also addressed the concept of a “kill switch” that could turn off AI if it became too potent, saying it was inadequate.
“It’s not enough to have a kill switch,” Gates remarked. “We’re not yet at the point where … they autonomously grab computers and, you know, can’t be shut down. So that discussion … just sort of shows how non-technical various people are.”
Gates otherwise is generally regarded as optimistic about humans’ future. Many reporting or commenting on his conversation with Welker noted that it occurred in the wake of a nearly 6,000-word essay that he published in late August warning about AI and the potentially lethal ills it poses to humanity on a large scale.
His fellow tech moguls including Sam Altman and Elon Musk have joined Gates in calling for a slowdown of the development of AI, which some experts theorize could precipitate the mass destruction of humans through bioweapons and nuclear war, among other methods.
Progressive US senator Bernie Sanders on 23 September proposed legislation that would temporarily pause advanced AI development while guardrails to the technology are put in place.
Meanwhile, Microsoft itself has been challenged for having a role in stoking some of the dystopian concerns surrounding AI.
Company employees and activists have organized a campaign aimed at getting Microsoft to cut ties with the Israeli military, which has used AI tools to kill in Gaza and – alongside US forces – in Iran, according to a Guardian essay published on Friday.
The essay’s authors, Mohamed Hussein and Granate Kim of the No Azure for Apartheid group, furthermore warned that “horrors wrought by AI” are also being seen in the US. For instance, the US Department of Homeland Security has used AI tools such as Microsoft’s Azure to monitor, arrest and deport immigrants en masse, Hussein and Kim wrote.
Gates’s essay in August and interview on Sunday were two of his first major forays into the public since becoming ensnared in the scandal surrounding Jeffrey Epstein, the disgraced financier who pleaded guilty in 2008 to procuring a minor for prostitution before dying by suicide while incarcerated on sex-trafficking charges 11 years later.
An external review commissioned by Gates’s philanthropic foundation and released in July determined that he was among a number of organization staffers and leaders who had collectively held about 30 meetings with Epstein from 2011 to 2014.
Gates has not been accused of involvement in Epstein’s admitted or alleged crimes. He has said he regretted “every minute” he spent with Epstein, and remains the chair of the $89bn (£65bn) Gates Foundation charity.
In a lighter moment during Welker’s interview with Gates, the host asked him: “Are there any ways in which you, professionally or personally, avoid AI and say that: ‘I’m not going to consult with it in this instance?’”
Gates, with a chuckle and a smile, replied: “Well, I’m not using it for my personal relationships. I’m not like: ‘Hey, do you like me? Hey, am I a nice guy?’
“So I just never went down that path, because I’m lucky in terms of my family, friends and everything. I don’t socialize with the AI. It knows I’m a very serious person.”
